title: 10 Kindle Formatting Mistakes That Get Your Book Rejected (And How to Fix Them)
excerpt: Most Kindle formatting mistakes are small and easy to fix. Here are the 10 that most often get indie books rejected or flagged by KDP, with a clear fix for each one.
meta_title: 10 Kindle Formatting Mistakes That Get Books Rejected | BookKraft AI
meta_description: Avoid the most common kindle formatting errors that cause KDP rejection. A practical ebook formatting guide for indie authors.
feature_image_alt: An author with her head in her hand, looking at a laptop showing a badly formatted ebook
html:
You uploaded your book to KDP. A day or two later, an email arrives. Something in the file is wrong, and the book isn't going live. Or it does go live, and a week later a reader leaves a review saying the chapters run together.

Formatting errors are one of the most common reasons KDP sends a book back. The good news is that most kindle formatting mistakes are small, and you can fix them yourself. You don't need to be a designer or a coder.

This ebook formatting guide covers ten kindle publishing mistakes that show up again and again in files from indie authors. For each one, you'll see what goes wrong, why it matters on a Kindle, and exactly how to fix it.

First, a quick word on how Kindle formatting works

A printed page always stays the same size. A Kindle screen doesn't. The reader picks the font, the text size, the line spacing and the background color, and the text flows to fit their screen. This is called reflowable text, and it's the reason kdp book formatting is so different from making a print PDF.

Almost every mistake below comes from the same root cause: formatting an ebook as if it were paper.

1. Pressing Enter to start a new page

In Word, it's tempting to tap Enter a few times until the next chapter lands on a fresh page. It looks right on your screen. On a Kindle, those empty lines stay put while the text around them moves. The result is chapters that start halfway down the screen, or blank screens in the middle of the book.

Fix: Delete the runs of empty paragraphs and use a real page break before each chapter. The easiest way is to turn on "Page break before" in your Heading 1 style, so every chapter title starts a new page by itself. Turn on formatting marks (the ¶ button in Word) to find empty lines you can't otherwise see. Our guide to ghost spacing in EPUB files shows what these blank lines look like once they're inside the file.

2. Using big bold text instead of real headings

Making a chapter title large and bold makes it look like a heading. But a Kindle doesn't read looks. It reads styles. If your chapter titles aren't set as Heading 1, the Kindle can't build a table of contents from them, and the Go To menu has nothing useful to show.

A missing or broken table of contents is one of the most common kindle formatting errors, and KDP can warn you about it at upload.

Fix: Apply Heading 1 to every chapter title and Heading 2 to sections inside chapters. Change how headings look by editing the style, never by formatting the text by hand. Then open your file in Kindle Previewer, tap Go To, and check that every chapter jumps where it should. If KDP already says it can't find your table of contents, our guide to the "No TOC Found" error walks you through it.

3. Indenting with tabs and spaces

Tabs and runs of spaces don't convert cleanly. Some e-readers drop them, and others show them as uneven gaps. Many authors also indent the first line and add a blank line between paragraphs. Both of those mean "new paragraph," so the book says it twice and looks homemade.

Fix: Pick one: a first-line indent, or a space between paragraphs. Set it once in your body paragraph style. Then use Find and Replace to remove the tabs and extra spaces that were doing the job by hand.

4. Locking the font size and page width

Some templates and export tools hard-code a font size in pixels or a fixed width for the text column. On a Kindle, that fights the reader. They turn the text size up and nothing changes, or the text runs off the edge of a small phone screen.

Fix: Let the reader control the surface. If you edit the CSS as part of your epub formatting, remove fixed font sizes and fixed widths, and use relative units such as em and percentages instead. Then read a full chapter with the text set two sizes bigger than you'd ever use, and see what falls apart.

5. Keeping headers, footers and page numbers

Running headers and page numbers are a print idea. A Kindle screen has no fixed pages to number, and the device already shows readers how far through the book they are. When headers or page numbers from a Word file sneak into an ebook, they can appear as stray lines in the middle of the text.

Fix: Keep headers, footers and page numbers in your print file only, and check that none of them made it into the ebook's body text. While you're at it, search for phrases like "see page 112." Page 112 doesn't exist on a Kindle, so turn each one into a link to the right spot.

6. Tables that are too wide for a phone

A five-column table fits nicely on a printed page. On a phone held upright, it gets squashed or cut off. The reader can't see the last columns, or the text wraps one word per line until the table is unreadable.

Fix: Keep tables to two or three columns where you can. Split a wide table into two smaller ones, or turn it into a list if the data allows. Then check every table on the smallest screen size in Kindle Previewer before you upload.

7. Images that are blurry, oversized or missing alt text

Images cause trouble in three ways. They can be too small and look blurry. They can be far too large and make the file heavy, which raises the delivery cost KDP takes from sales at the 70% royalty rate. Or they can disappear completely because a file path broke during export, leaving a gray box where the picture should be.

Then there's alt text, the short description a screen reader speaks aloud for readers who can't see the image. KDP now asks whether your images are accessible when you publish, and accessibility rules for ebooks sold in the EU took effect in June 2025.

Fix: Use clear images sized for the screen, not files straight from a camera. Keep every image inside the EPUB, named exactly as the text refers to it. Write alt text for every image that carries information: one sentence that says what the image tells the reader. Give purely decorative images an empty alt so screen readers skip them.

8. Links that point to the wrong place

Two kinds of links cause problems. The first is a link that goes nowhere, such as one aimed at a page number or a heading that was later renamed. Tapping it does nothing, and readers notice. The second is more serious: a link to a competing bookstore. KDP restricts links to other retailers in Kindle books, and they can get a book blocked or removed from sale.

Fix: Point internal links at bookmarks, not page numbers. Tap every single link in Kindle Previewer. Internal links should jump, web links should open, and none should send readers to another bookstore. If you sell your book in several stores, make a separate ebook file for each one.

9. Special characters that turn into boxes

Curly quotes, accented names, dashes and symbols can show up as empty boxes, question marks or strange strings like "â€™". There are usually two causes. An empty box often means the font doesn't include that character. Garbled strings usually mean the file was saved with the wrong text encoding.

Fix: Save your manuscript and every HTML file as UTF-8. Rebuild the book, then check every accented name, quotation mark and symbol you use. If a character still shows as a box, switch to a common font or replace that character.

10. A cover and metadata that don't match

This one catches a lot of first-time authors. The title or subtitle on the cover says one thing, and the title typed into the KDP form says another. Maybe a word is missing, or the subtitle words are in a different order. KDP compares the two, and a mismatch can stop your book from going live.

Fix: Type the title, subtitle and author name into KDP exactly as they appear on your cover, word for word. Do the same for series names and edition numbers. Then check them one last time before you press Publish.

How to catch kindle formatting mistakes before KDP does

You don't have to find every problem by eye. A short routine catches most of them:

  1. Validate the file. Run your EPUB through a validator, such as the free BookKraft AI EPUB Validator. It lists broken structure, missing files and markup errors in plain language.
  2. Preview it on several screens. Kindle Previewer is free from Amazon. Check your book as a phone, a tablet and an e-reader, with the text size turned up.
  3. Read one chapter on a real device. A previewer is close, but nothing beats holding the book the way your readers will.
  4. Check the listing. Compare your cover with the title, subtitle and author fields in KDP before you publish.

If your problem is inside the EPUB file itself, see our list of EPUB formatting mistakes that get books rejected and our guide to why KDP rejects EPUB files.

Ten mistakes is a solid start. Real books run into many more: drop caps that break, poems that lose their line breaks, fonts that won't embed, and spine widths that don't add up.
